extracted.intended_audience: artists, art students, aestheticians, psychologists, and educated general readers interested in visual aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and explanatory guidance for judging what makes a visual form pleasing or beautiful, focusing on perceptual, associative, and formal principles (unity, continuity, proportion, symmetry, tactile/muscular associations, skill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity in variety (order among manifold details)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty of form — so far as it is independent of sensuous pleasure ... and pleasures of association and suggestion — is resolvable into the presence of a certain order among manifold details, which order is commonly spoken of as unity in variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'unity in variety' as the core standard: a pleasing design shows ordered relations among diverse elements. Use this as an overarching criterion that other principles (continuity, centrality, similarity) serve to achieve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of parts / contour
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuity of lines into pleasing form: a continuous as opposed to a broken arrangement is at once felt to be a unity; the movement of the eye around a contour yields a peculiar feeling of gratification called a sense of completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether contours and continuous lines facilitate smooth ocular movement and a sense of completion. Examples: accentuated contour in decorative designs. Note: continuity is often developed by experience and aids unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common correlation with a dominant central element (centrality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common connection with one principal element of form, more particularly with a dominant central feature — the arrangement of parts about a center supplies the most natural mode of percipient activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether parts relate to a clear central element (point, line, axis). Radiating, circular, and axial arrangements (trees, flowers, scrolls) are particularly pleasing. Recognize that the central element is sometimes only 'supplied by the mind' (ideal completion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity and equality of parts (direction, proportion, equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity of parts includes likeness of direction, equality of magnitudes, proportion, etc.; pleasing forms present similarities of direction, simple and compound, and beauty is often traceable to a prominent element of direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge directional consistency, equalities, proportional relations among elements. Note that proportion may be apprehended vaguely rather than numerically; the eye precisely estimates relative magnitudes even if not consciously calculating ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry (especially bilateral symmetry) and its appropriate use
rubrics_metrics.description: A symmetrical division of parts aims at presenting continuous features under contrast and similarity in relation to a center. Bilateral symmetry is frequently used in art; perfect symmetry may be 'too stiffly regular' for art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use symmetry as a criterion for unity and balance, but penalize overly rigid symmetry when variety or freedom is desired. Bilateral (horizontal) symmetry tends to please more than other directions; consider cultural/habitual bases of this preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and the (possible) aesthetic value of particular ratios (e.g., the golden section)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations of proportion enter into beautiful form; technical eyes may recognize simple numerical ratios among magnitudes; Zeising's 'golden section' may supply a special aesthetic value though appreciation is often vague, not numerical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate overall proportional balance and whether ratios feel 'right' even if viewers can't name them. Consider empirical evidence (Fechner) but be cautious: conscious numerical appreciation is rare; preference may be habitual or derived from human-figure norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal completion / subjective restoration and tolerance of approximation
rubrics_metrics.description: The uniting element is often present in an ideal manner only, suggested to the mind rather than directly presented; the eye can be satisfied when there is only an approximation to a regular arrangement provided it appears intended and justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow for implied centers, contours, or completions (e.g., a crescent expanded mentally to a circle). Do not penalize deliberate approximations; mark as flaw only when departures look like errors or bad workmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ocular-motor factors (pleasure from eye movement, direction preferences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce continuity of lines into pleasing form in the nature of ocular movement; the eye's preference for directions (horizontal, movements from center) and the gratification from tracing contours are direct sensuous factors in visual form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether design supports comfortable, natural eye movements (horizontal preference, center-focused tracing). Consider retinal/mechanical explanations (overlap on same retinal meridian) when analyzing why certain layouts please.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associated tactual and muscular suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic aspects depending on association with touch and movement: pleasures of visual form often derive from tactual and muscular experiences (vertical vs horizontal, curve vs straight line, smoothness of surface).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider implied tactile/muscular qualities — does a form suggest smoothness, resistance, repose, or movement in ways that add to its appeal? Examples: 'bossiness' in sculpture, voluptuous curves vs severe straight lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestion of human skill / workmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Associated appreciation of human skill: perfectly straight lines and perfect regularity call up a consciousness of artistic finish; departures that suggest bad workmanship are unpleasant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate perceived craftsmanship and finish. Reward evidence of fine workmanship or purposeful finish; penalize irregularities that read as unskilled mistakes rather than intentional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associations to human and organic forms (figurative associations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete associations depending on resemblance to agreeable natural forms, especially the human figure; human presence supplies supreme interest and we readily see analogies to human attitude in inanimate forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note whether forms evoke human or organic associations that enhance aesthetic value (columns suggesting caryatids, plant-like ornament). Use such associations as positive factors unless they produce inappropriate anthropomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of asymmetry and controlled irregularity for artistic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristic effect of asymmetry (e.g., many Japanese designs) is due to a just feeling for form; irregularities owe their piquancy to the sense of a law that is broken, though not violently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize deliberate asymmetry or 'discords' as valid devices to create interest or 'piquancy' when controlled. Penalize irregularity only if it appears to be an error or unmotivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative weighting of direct sensuous vs associated factors (no strict quantitative measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychology is not yet a quantitative science; aesthetics must be content with enumerating elements without seeking to measure exactly their relative values. Direct sensuous elements (ocular movement) and associated elements (touch, skill, associations) both contribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging overall aesthetic value, consider multiple contributing factors rather than a single metric. Explicit numerical scoring is inappropriate; use balanced qualitative assessment noting which factors dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual subordinations (form vs imitation / functional demands)
rubrics_metrics.description: In some arts (painting) form is subordinate to imitation and picturesque variety; in sculpture regularity may be sacrificed for natural ease; the best art often disguises form and appeals to imaginative reconstruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate form relative to the medium's primary aims (e.g., imitation in painting, tactile qualities in sculpture). Do not demand identical formal criteria across media; consider whether form serves imitation, function, or expressive ends appropriately.
